title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Low union rates in Louisiana show workers prefer going it alone

Rebuttal: Some workers do prefer that. But Louisiana's union rate rose from 3.9% to 4.4% in 2025, and surveys show many nonunion workers would join if they could. Fear of retaliation and right-to-work keep numbers down.

Sources: BLS Union Members by State 2026, Kochan et al., MIT 2018

title: Claude Drop: labor-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Workers are paid what they're worth in a free market

Rebuttal: Markets do set many wages. But markets also reflect who has power. Labor's share at a record low means owners captured more of what workers produced. Where workers bargain together, they get closer to what they're worth.

Sources: BLS Productivity and Costs 2026, BLS Union Members 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Labor's share of income in the nonfarm business sector fell to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest in a series that began in 1947

Workers' slice of what business produces has never been smaller. That's not a market accident. It's a power gap.

Source: BLS Productivity and Costs, Sept. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Real hourly compensation in the nonfarm business sector fell at a 3.3% annual rate in the second quarter of 2026

Productivity rose 1.4% that quarter. Workers produced more and got paid less in real terms.

Source: BLS Productivity and Costs, Sept. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
In 2025, nonfarm business productivity rose 2.2% while real hourly compensation rose 1.4%

Even in a decent year, pay trailed output. The gap goes somewhere, and it isn't your paycheck.

Source: BLS Productivity and Costs, March 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Median weekly earnings for full-time workers were $1,251 in the second quarter of 2026, up 4.6% from a year earlier, while consumer prices rose 3.9%

Most of the raise went to the grocery store and the landlord. What's left is pocket change.

Source: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings, July 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Real median weekly earnings were $378 in 1982–84 dollars in the second quarter of 2026, up from $376 a year earlier

Two dollars a week in real terms. That's the gain for a year of full-time work.

Source: BLS via FRED, series LES1252881600Q, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Women working full time earned a median $1,131 a week in the second quarter of 2026, 82.0% of men's $1,380

The gap costs women about $249 every week. Union contracts with posted pay scales shrink it.

Source: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings, July 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Black full-time workers earned a median $1,029 a week in the second quarter of 2026, compared with $1,268 for white workers

A $239 weekly gap. Solidarity across race lines is how working people close it.

Source: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings, July 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Full-time workers at the 10th percentile earned $642 a week in the second quarter of 2026; those at the 90th earned $2,924

The top tenth earns over four times the bottom tenth. Raising the floor matters most.

Source: BLS Usual Weekly Earnings, July 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division recovered more than $259 million in back wages for nearly 177,000 workers in fiscal 2025

That's about $1,465 per worker, the most since 2019. And that's only what investigators caught.

Source: U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division, Jan. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
EPI found that federal, state and local efforts recovered more than $1.5 billion in stolen wages from 2021 to 2023

Billions recovered, and researchers say it's a sliver of the total. Wage theft is routine, not rare.

Source: Economic Policy Institute 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana is one of seven states where the state labor agency does not recover unpaid wages for workers, according to EPI

If your boss stiffs you in Louisiana, the state won't chase it. Workers have to rely on federal investigators, courts and each other.

Source: Economic Policy Institute 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Labor Department found 5,272 minors employed in violation of child labor laws in fiscal 2025, up from 1,012 in fiscal 2015

More than five times as many kids in a decade. Enforcement is finding a crisis, not creating one.

Source: U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division, child labor data, FY2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Labor Department found 773 minors illegally employed in hazardous occupations in fiscal 2025, up from 365 the year before

Hazardous means saws, slaughter lines and heavy machinery. Children don't belong there.

Source: U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division, FY2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
At least 13 states introduced bills to weaken child labor protections in 2026, and several, including West Virginia and Indiana, enacted them

While violations climb, lawmakers are loosening the rules. That's the wrong direction.

Source: Economic Policy Institute, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Arkansas eliminated work permit requirements for children under 16 in 2023

Permits were a simple check on who's hiring kids and for what. Removing them made exploitation easier to hide.

Source: Arkansas Youth Hiring Act of 2023

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Federal OSHA would need about 191 years to inspect each U.S. workplace once, up from 84 years in 1991 (AFL-CIO calculation)

Most workplaces will never see an inspector. Safety depends on workers speaking up together.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
About 1,651 federal and state OSHA inspectors covered roughly 155 million workers, one inspector per 93,877 workers (AFL-CIO calculation)

In 1991 it was one per 54,952. The workforce grew. The watchdogs shrank.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The average federal OSHA penalty for a serious violation was $4,678 in fiscal 2025

A serious violation means it could kill or badly hurt someone. The fine is less than a month's rent in some cities.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The median federal OSHA penalty in a worker death case was $16,550 in fiscal 2025

A worker's life, valued below a used truck. Families deserve real accountability.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Only 144 worker death cases have been criminally prosecuted under the Occupational Safety and Health Act since 1970

Thousands die on the job every year. Almost no one ever faces a criminal court for it.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
An estimated 530 workers died from heat on the job in 2024 (estimate)

Heat deaths are often misrecorded, so the real toll is higher. Every one is preventable with water, rest and shade.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
OSHA proposed a federal heat injury and illness prevention rule on Aug. 30, 2024, and has taken no step toward finalizing it since comments closed in October 2025

Two Gulf summers and counting with no federal rule. Workers can't wait on paperwork.

Source: Federal Register 2024; Ogletree Deakins 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Seven states have their own heat illness prevention standards: California, Colorado, Maryland, Minnesota, Nevada, Oregon and Washington

Louisiana, one of the hottest states, isn't on the list. Our legislators could change that.

Source: Ogletree Deakins, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Workers age 65 and older died on the job at 9.1 per 100,000 in 2024, nearly three times the overall rate

People working past retirement age are dying at work. A real retirement is a safety issue.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026, from BLS data

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The death rate for young workers rose to 2.7 per 100,000 in 2024, up from 1.3 in 2022

More young people are dying on the job. Training and the right to refuse unsafe work save lives.

Source: AFL-CIO, Death on the Job 2026, from BLS data

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana recorded 96 fatal work injuries in 2024, a rate of 5.1 per 100,000 full-time workers

Above the national rate of 3.3. Ninety-six families got the call nobody wants.

Source: BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Fatal work injuries among Hispanic or Latino workers in Louisiana rose from 12 in 2023 to 22 in 2024

The people rebuilding our roofs and refineries are dying at higher numbers. Their safety is our safety.

Source: BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
In March 2026, 63% of the lowest-paid quarter of civilian workers had paid sick leave, compared with 95% of the highest-paid quarter

The workers who handle our food and care for our elders are the least likely to get a sick day.

Source: BLS National Compensation Survey, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
49% of private-industry workers had access to paid family leave in March 2026

Half the workforce gets nothing paid when a baby is born or a parent is dying.

Source: BLS National Compensation Survey, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
In March 2026, 48% of the lowest-paid quarter of private-industry workers had access to a retirement plan and 22% participated; for the highest-paid quarter it was 92% and 81%

Retirement in America is a benefit for the well-paid. Union contracts extend it to everyone.

Source: BLS National Compensation Survey, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The FTC voted 3-1 in September 2025 to dismiss its appeals and accept the vacatur of its 2024 rule banning most noncompete agreements

The ban never took effect. Workers have to rely on state laws and collective bargaining.

Source: Federal Trade Commission, Sept. 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Labor Department told investigators in May 2025 to stop enforcing its 2024 independent contractor rule, and proposed replacing it in February 2026

Misclassification strips minimum wage and overtime. Washington just made it easier.

Source: U.S. DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-1; DOL proposed rule, Feb. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Nineteen states raised their minimum wages on Jan. 1, 2026, raising pay for more than 8.3 million workers by about $5 billion a year

Raises came from voters and organizers, not from Congress.

Source: Economic Policy Institute, Dec. 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Twenty states with about 60.2 million workers still used the $7.25 federal minimum wage in 2026

Most are in the South. Louisiana is one of them. Same country, two wage floors.

Source: Economic Policy Institute, Dec. 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Washington state's minimum wage was $17.13 an hour in 2026, versus $7.25 in Louisiana

That's a $9.88 an hour gap, more than $20,000 a year for a full-time worker.

Source: Economic Policy Institute, Dec. 2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
U.S. workers took part in 30 major work stoppages in 2025, involving 306,800 workers, up 13% from 2024

BLS counts only strikes of 1,000 or more. Workers are using their power more often.

Source: BLS Major Work Stoppages, Feb. 2026; EPI 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Cornell's Labor Action Tracker counted 303 work stoppages involving about 290,000 workers in 2025

Hundreds of strikes, most of them small. Every one started with coworkers deciding together.

Source: ILR-LER Labor Action Tracker Annual Report 2025, Cornell University

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Health care and social assistance workers made up about 40% of workers on strike in 2025

Nurses and aides are striking over staffing. Short staffing hurts patients as much as workers.

Source: ILR-LER Labor Action Tracker Annual Report 2025, Cornell University

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The South had 43 work stoppages involving about 6,760 workers in 2025, the fewest of any U.S. region

Low strike activity reflects weak labor laws, not happy workers. Southern pay shows it.

Source: ILR-LER Labor Action Tracker Annual Report 2025, Cornell University

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The NLRB lacked a quorum for 345 days after the president fired board member Gwynne Wilcox on Jan. 27, 2025

Nearly a year when the board couldn't decide cases. Justice delayed hit workers fired for organizing.

Source: Center for American Progress, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
NLRB-supervised union elections fell 30% in 2025, to 1,498 from 2,124 in 2024, while unions won 69.8% of them

Fewer elections, but workers still won most. The appetite is there.

Source: Center for American Progress, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Supreme Court overruled Humphrey's Executor 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter on June 29, 2026, expanding presidential power to remove independent agency members

Labor law enforcement now swings harder with each election. Workers' strongest protection is their own organization.

Source: U.S. Supreme Court, Trump v. Slaughter, 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
4.4% of Louisiana wage and salary workers were union members in 2025, up from 3.9% in 2024

Small but growing. Every percentage point is thousands of workers with a contract.

Source: BLS Union Members by State, Jan. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The average hourly wage in the New Orleans-Metairie area was $29.35 in May 2025, about 12.5% below the national average of $33.54

Our city runs on hospitality and the people doing that work are paid far under the nation.

Source: BLS Occupational Employment and Wages, Aug. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
New Orleans-area waiters and waitresses averaged $11.55 an hour in May 2025

The workers who make this city's reputation are among its lowest paid.

Source: BLS Occupational Employment and Wages, Aug. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Production workers in the Baton Rouge area averaged $33.04 an hour in May 2025, compared with $24.81 nationally

Skilled plant work with real bargaining leverage pays. Leverage is the lesson.

Source: BLS Occupational Employment and Wages, Aug. 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Foreign-born workers made up 19.1% of the U.S. civilian labor force in 2025

Nearly one in five workers. Divide them from native-born workers and every paycheck sinks.

Source: BLS Labor Force Characteristics of Foreign-born Workers, May 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Full-time foreign-born workers earned a median $1,059 a week in 2025, 85.7% of the $1,236 earned by native-born workers

Underpaying immigrants is a tool to underpay everyone. Equal standards protect all workers.

Source: BLS Labor Force Characteristics of Foreign-born Workers, May 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Labor Department certified 398,258 H-2A guest worker positions in fiscal 2025, including 14,631 in Louisiana

Guest workers' visas are tied to their employer. That makes speaking up dangerous and abuse easier.

Source: U.S. DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification, FY2025

title: Claude Drop: labor-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Angola farm line workers become eligible for pay of 2 to 4 cents an hour after three years of unpaid work

Field work on a former plantation for pennies. Louisiana should end it.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, May 2026

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What does it mean that labor's share hit a record low?

It means the pie got bigger and our slice got smaller. BLS says workers' share of income in the nonfarm business sector fell to 52.8% in spring 2026. That's the lowest since records began in 1947. We made the money. Somebody else kept it.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Explain labor share like I'm a welder on my lunch break.

Every dollar your plant brings in gets split two ways: paychecks and owners. Right now workers' cut is the smallest BLS has ever measured, back to 1947. You didn't get lazier. They got greedier. And nobody hands that slice back unless we organize.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Wages went up 4.6% this year. Isn't that good news?

It's real, and I'll take it. Median weekly pay hit $1,251 in spring 2026, up 4.6%. But prices rose 3.9%. After inflation, the typical full-time worker gained about two bucks a week. That's not a raise. That's treading water.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Give me a 20-second radio answer on why wages feel stuck.

Because they are. After inflation, typical weekly pay barely moved in a year, about two dollars. Meanwhile workers' share of the economy just hit the lowest level BLS has ever recorded. We're producing more and keeping less. The fix is old and it works: a union contract with your name on it.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
How much did the Labor Department recover in stolen wages last year?

More than $259 million in fiscal 2025, for nearly 177,000 workers. That's about $1,465 a person. Think about that. Rent money, car notes, school clothes, taken by bosses who got caught. Most never do.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Is wage theft really a big deal or just a few bad apples?

It's a business model. The Labor Department alone recovered over $259 million last year, and that's only the cases they found with a shrinking staff. Unpaid overtime, shaved hours, stolen tips. When stealing is cheap, it spreads. Organized workers make it expensive.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What can Louisiana workers do about wage theft?

Start with the facts: EPI found Louisiana is one of seven states where the state doesn't recover unpaid wages for workers. So keep your own records. Photograph schedules and pay stubs. Call the federal Wage and Hour line, 866-487-9243. And talk to coworkers, because one complaint is a case and twenty is a movement.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Why are kids getting hurt at work again?

Because enforcement found 5,272 minors working illegally in fiscal 2025, five times the number from a decade earlier. 773 of them were in jobs the law calls hazardous. Meanwhile states are loosening child labor laws. Kids belong in school and on ball fields, not on kill floors at 2 a.m.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What's going on with state child labor laws?

A rollback. Arkansas scrapped work permits for kids under 16 in 2023. In 2026 alone, at least 13 states filed bills to weaken protections, and West Virginia wiped out its list of banned hazardous jobs for minors. Who benefits? Employers who want cheap, quiet labor. Who pays? Children.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
How long would it take OSHA to inspect every workplace?

The AFL-CIO calculates 191 years for federal OSHA to visit each workplace once. In 1991 it was 84 years. There are about 1,651 inspectors for 155 million workers. That's not a safety system. That's a lottery where you're the ticket.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
What's the penalty when a boss gets a worker killed?

The AFL-CIO found the median OSHA penalty in a worker death case was $16,550 in fiscal 2025. A life, priced below a used pickup. Only 144 worker death cases have been criminally prosecuted under the OSH Act since 1970. Families deserve more than a fine and a form letter.

title: Claude Drop: labor-karl_voice
author: Claude
text:
Is there a federal heat rule for workers yet?

No. OSHA proposed one in August 2024. Comments closed in October 2025. Since then, nothing has moved toward a final rule. Only seven states have their own heat standards, and Louisiana isn't one. Water, rest and shade shouldn't depend on your boss's mood.
